To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) for any system of treatment contrasts, there is a graph that represents this system, and (2) the optimal designs for estimating this system are represented by the inverses (or, in general, powers) of the vertex weights of the corresponding graph, which are determined using the eigenvalues of the vertex-weight matrix of the graph and its Laplacian matrix.

(i) the eigenvalue-based optimal approximate designs can be expressed as inverses of vertex weights in the vertex-weighted graph representing the system of treatment contrasts, and (ii) the Laplacians and the eigenvalues of the vertex-weight graphs can be used to obtain the optimal designs and their optimality criteria.

(i) the optimal approximate designs can be represented by graphs, (ii) the optimality criteria can then be interpreted in terms of graph theory, and (iii) the optimality results for symmetric systems of pairwise contrasts can be extended to other systems of treatment contrasts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following topics.
optimal designs for treatment comparisons, and we provide a new representation of these designs by graphs.
the design of experiments for comparing a set treatments.

for the estimation of treatment contrasts, the optimality criteria of D-optimality and A-optimality are equivalent, while E-optimality is a more restrictive criterion.
the graph representation is an effective tool for obtaining optimality results for the estimation of systems of contrasts in a variety of settings.

, for any system of treatment contrasts, the corresponding optimal approximate design can be represented by a vertex-weighted graph and the values of optimality criteria for the design can be expressed using graph theoretic properties of the graph.

the optimal designs for treatment comparisons are determined by the graph representation of the corresponding systems of treatment contrasts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the optimality of designs for the comparison of treatments in an experiment can be determined using the graph theory.
the optimal designs for the estimation problem of treatment contrasts can be obtained from the optimal designs for a corresponding estimation problem of treatment means.
optimal treatment proportions can be found using a simple algorithm that involves the eigenvalues of a graph.
